other_side: Zitron's answer to the idea that the subsidy war is a gift is that the gift is the whole con. Subscription demand, he argues, only exists because labs sell what he calls '$40 for a dollar' — the very Semi Analysis figures NLW celebrates are, for him, proof there is no real business underneath, just venture capital funnelled through OpenAI and Anthropic to hyperscalers and NVIDIA. Demand is 'decidedly artificial', manufactured by media consent and free compute, and it will vanish the moment the discount does. His conclusion is blunt: when the bubble pops, 'no bailouts, no handouts' — an industry propped up by subsidy is unworthy of rescue and should be allowed to burn.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is the subsidy — the gap between what a token costs to serve and what a subscriber pays. Neither disputes the facts: both cite Semi Analysis's finding that a $200 monthly plan can burn up to $14,000 of compute. The empirical question, which will resolve, is whether inference costs fall fast enough for today's prices to turn profitable before the capital funding the gap runs out; the observable that settles it is what happens to rate limits and subscription prices over the next year, and whether usage survives the change. The residue is pure worldview: is subsidised usage seeding durable demand or manufacturing fake demand? NLW is vindicated if costs collapse and users stay at honest prices; Zitron if usage retreats the moment the discount does. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW sells daily bullishness to builders, Zitron sells bubble certainty to sceptics — so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: today's prices are unsustainable as charged. Watch the first frontier lab to materially tighten limits or raise prices, and what its users do next.
